---
title: "Tree-based"
---

Tree-based models make predictions by repeatedly dividing the feature space
into smaller regions. Within each final region, a regression tree predicts an
average response and a classification tree predicts a class frequency.

## 1. Decision trees from scratch

**Estimated time:** 45–60 minutes

Build the first two splits of a high-CO decision tree from the gas-turbine
measurements. Compute Gini impurity, search across features and cutpoints, and
then use scikit-learn to draw the same shallow tree.

[View the notebook](01-decision-trees-from-scratch.ipynb)

## 2. How a decision tree grows

**Estimated time:** 5–10 minutes

Watch a simple two-feature classification tree add one conditional rule at a
time. See how each split creates a local decision region and the corresponding
decision process.

[Open the interactive animation](02-tree-growth-animation.qmd)

Use a small labeled dataset to see how a tree evaluates every available
cutpoint with weighted Gini impurity, then chooses the best one.

[Explore how a tree chooses a split](03-gini-split-explorer.qmd)

Watch a more mingled version of the mock data continue splitting until it
classifies every training observation correctly. See how a perfect training fit
can require increasingly local rules.

[Watch the overfitting animation](04-tree-overfitting-animation.qmd)

## 3. Bagging

**Estimated time:** 30–40 minutes

See how bootstrap samples create different decision trees, how their predictions
are averaged, and why the resulting ensemble has stronger held-out performance
than one fully grown tree.

[View the notebook](05-bagging.ipynb)

Use real bootstrap samples, fitted tree roots, individual tree votes, and
held-out AUC to watch a bagged ensemble grow one tree at a time.

[Explore bagging](05-bagging-explorer.qmd)

## 4. Random forests

**Estimated time:** 40–50 minutes

See how averaging many fully grown trees can stabilize predictions, and how
random feature subsets make the trees less alike. We compare one tree, bagging,
and a random forest on the same gas-turbine classification task.

[View the notebook](05-random-forests.ipynb)

Use actual fitted gas-turbine models to watch individual tree votes, the
running ensemble probability, root-feature diversity, and held-out AUC evolve
as a forest grows.

[Explore a random forest](06-random-forest-explorer.qmd)

## 5. AdaBoost

See how AdaBoost trains a sequence of shallow trees on the same
gas-turbine observations. Each new stump gives more influence to observations
missed by the earlier stumps, and the final model pools their weighted votes.

[View the notebook](07-adaboost.ipynb)

Use fitted stumps to see how each round shifts observation weight, contributes
a weighted vote for one new observation, and changes held-out AUC.

[Explore AdaBoost](07-adaboost-explorer.qmd)

## 6. Gradient boosting

See how gradient boosting starts with one mean NOx prediction, then adds small
regression trees that correct the current model's residuals. Unlike AdaBoost,
it does not reweight observations: each tree adds a continuous correction to
the current prediction.

[View the notebook](08-gradient-boosting.ipynb)

[Explore gradient boosting](08-gradient-boosting-explorer.qmd)
